problem: Robotic guide-dog research lacks open, user-grounded specifications of what BLV travelers need, and existing guide robots depend on LiDAR/GPS/dense metric maps that are costly, heavy, power-hungry and fragile in rain, glass and urban settings. Visual teach-and-repeat is also fragile to scene changes between teach and repeat runs.
motivation: Design decisions such as sensor suite, runtime, route length and terrain depend on how BLV users actually travel with guide dogs, but open data on this is scarce. Guide dogs repeat familiar routes taught to them, which suggests a lightweight, vision-only teach-and-repeat framework that suits daily routine routes.
key_idea: A vision-only teach-and-repeat guide robot that stores a sparse topological map of DINOv3-selected keyframes, localizes via CosPlace place recognition with temporal Bayesian filtering, and steers using Reloc3r relative pose regression to the next keyframe.
insight: Requirements drawn from the formative study (GuideData) justify dropping LiDAR/GPS/depth, and chaining short visually guided segments avoids drift accumulation and copes with lighting and object changes. The component comparisons are qualitative only (no numbers): learned embeddings beat a distance heuristic for keyframe selection, and direct pose regression beat feature matching+PnP, which failed on textureless and very bright scenes. Users' reactions show feasibility, while trainers' criticism (robotic, abrupt motion, missing body cues) exposes a usability gap versus real guide dogs.
method: Formative study / GuideData: interviews with 26 guide dog handlers, 4 cane users, 9 trainers and 1 O&M trainer plus 15+ h of observation, released as de-identified data (39 transcripts, 31 images, 126 videos) and used to derive hardware and navigation requirements.

Topological map generator: teleoperated teach run; each frame is encoded by DINOv3 into an L2-normalized descriptor, and an adaptive selector enforces minimum temporal spacing, appearance diversity over a recent buffer and adaptive similarity thresholds, giving about 24 MB per km; optional manual removal of blurry keyframes.

Visual place recognition with temporal consistency: CosPlace 512-d descriptors, cosine-similarity retrieval of subgoals, and a Bayesian belief update over topological nodes (following PlaceNav) to avoid erratic switching and the kidnapping problem.

Relative pose estimation: Reloc3r-512 regresses the SE(3) transform between the current image and the subgoal keyframe, projected to the ground plane as (dx, dy, dyaw), with mixed-precision inference.

Controller: unicycle model with polar coordinates (rho, alpha, beta), a nonlinear feedback law v = vmax(1-exp(-k_rho*rho)), w = k_alpha*alpha + k_beta*beta, plus heuristics (slow near goal, damping under large heading error, amplified final orientation correction, velocity limits). There is no local planner.
Platform: Unitree Go2 with rigid harness handle, single RealSense D435i RGB camera, running at 5 Hz on a Jetson AGX Orin.

Stakeholder evaluation: robot-solo field tests over five environments, plus trials with 3 BLV guide dog handlers and a blindfolded trainer on a standard guide dog evaluation course, with NASA-TLX, SUS and interviews.

setting.backbone: DINOv3 (keyframe selection), CosPlace (place recognition), Reloc3r-512 (relative pose); all pretrained, used as-is
setting.training_data: none (pretrained foundation models used without additional training); the map is built from a single teach demonstration per route
setting.observation: monocular RGB (single Intel RealSense D435i, no depth used)
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity (v, w) on a unicycle model
setting.privileged: none at repeat time (a human teleoperates the teach run and may manually filter keyframes)

numbers.eval_set_note: 5 routes (FidelcoFront->Storage, FidelcoFront->Parking, LongWalkLoop, ResidentialLoop, ClassroomLoop-Indoor), no user
numbers.extra: teach-and-repeat on the same route, different day/time; Go2 + Jetson AGX Orin
numbers.evidence: Table 'Robot Solo and Handler-Guide Dog Robot Team Navigation Results', Total: 45/50 (90%), 2420 m, 1 collision, 10 interventions

numbers.eval_set_note: 8 trials with H01, H02, H03 (BLV handlers) and T02 (blindfolded trainer)
numbers.extra: human in the harness; the 6 interventions exclude technical malfunctions (camera disconnection/overheating)
numbers.evidence: Table 'Robot Solo and Handler-Guide Dog Robot Team Navigation Results', Total: 46/46 (100%), 4940 m, 1 collision, 6 interventions

numbers_note: Component ablations (keyframe selection, DINOv3 vs distance heuristic, Reloc3r vs feature matching+PnP) are described qualitatively only, with no numbers. No standard navigation benchmarks are used. Table distances appear to be cumulative route lengths per row, so the totals should be read with care.
results: Robot-solo runs achieved a 90% turning success rate (45/50) over 2420 m with 1 collision and 10 interventions. With BLV handlers and trainers, 46/46 turns succeeded (100%) over 4940 m with 6 interventions and 1 collision, including a 2.02 km round trip. BLV handlers gave low workload and high SUS (92.5 and 95.0 for two of them), while the trainer rated it 52.5 SUS against her 80.0 benchmark for a guide dog. No baseline navigation systems are compared numerically.
limitations: No quantitative baseline comparisons or ablation numbers; only 3 BLV users and 1 blindfolded trainer, on familiar routes only

Relies on a human teach run and manual keyframe filtering, has no local planner (needs guidance interventions for unexpected obstacles), and motion is abrupt and 'robotic' with no body cues, no landmark or curb signaling
Technical malfunctions (camera disconnection/overheating) occurred, and one user (H02) rated usability low
